executive_summary: CAD/JPY closed at 112.804 on 30 October 2026. That price is the number of yen per Canadian dollar, so a rising pair means a stronger CAD. The pair is up 1.48% over one month and 0.56% over three months, down 1.79% over six months and up 2.06% over a year. It sits at the 49th percentile of its 52-week closing range of 108.521–117.244. Two forces dominate the pair, and they pull in opposite directions. First, the energy shock pushes the pair up through both currencies: WTI is near USD 102 and JKM LNG near USD 33, which helps Canada as an oil exporter and drains yen through Japan's import bill. Second, the 125bp policy gap is likely to narrow. The Bank of Japan has two scheduled chances to hike inside the strategic horizon (18 December and the 22 January Outlook Report meeting), while the Bank of Canada's only decision is a probable hold on 9 December. Neither dossier captures one point on its own: speculators are short CAD and long yen at the same time, which makes CAD/JPY a crowded short. Positioning risk therefore points up even as the rate story points down. The tactical stance is Neutral, conviction 2, with a weighted score of +0.0448. The strategic stance is Bearish, conviction 2, with a score of −0.1301, only 0.03 past the threshold. The plan is to stay flat through the 6–20 November data cluster, then sell rallies into the 113.35–113.85 confluence of the 100-day average and four-touch resistance. The stop is a daily close above 114.65, the targets are 111.80 and 110.75 by late January, and the six-month expectation is 110.20, where the rising 200-week average is due to meet price. The main caveat is that the bearish rate case and the bullish oil case are linked through the Gulf: a lasting escalation would remove the edge.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On World Bank PPP factors, fair value for CAD/JPY is about 83.21. That leaves CAD 35.6% expensive against the yen, or the yen 26.2% cheap against CAD (flagged in both dossiers as best available). Both currencies are cheap in real effective terms. The yen is far cheaper: its BIS real effective rate is 66.61, the lowest in G10+SGD by 26.8 points, against CAD's 95.59, which is at the 3rd percentile of its own window. At 112.80 the market prices a yen that stays penalised by negative real rates and the energy bill, and a CAD discounted for tariffs. Valuation therefore argues for a lower CAD/JPY over the long run. It has no mean-reversion clock inside six months and does not enter any factor stance.

market_context.recent_regime: The pair is trading the energy war against Japanese normalisation. From late July to 30 September it fell more than 500 pips as joint US–Japan intervention and hawkish Bank of Japan commentary hit the yen leg. Through October it recovered toward 112.80 as WTI rose 14.1% and the Bank of Canada hiked on 28 October. This year commentators have described CAD/JPY as a pair where the oil shock works twice, with CAD strength and JPY weakness being driven by same underlying shock. The same analysis warned that actual intervention would likely trigger broad Yen buying across crosses, while a BoJ hike would challenge carry mechanism more fundamentally. That tension is the one this report trades.

bilateral_carry_analysis.breakeven_move: 125bp a year is about 141 pips a year at 112.804: about 11 pips over four weeks, 35 pips over three months and 70 pips over six months. A short position must fall at least that far to cover carry.
bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: A long CAD/JPY position earns +125bp a year (Bank of Canada 2.50% minus Bank of Japan 1.25%). The rolled futures premium between the November and December CME Canadian dollar and yen futures, crossed and observed 29 October, is −123.7bp a year; it combines the interest differential and the cross-currency basis, and because it is close to the policy gap the CAD-versus-yen basis looks near zero. The carry-to-vol ratio is 0.185 (125bp over the 6.764% estimated three-month vol); because that vol is a floor, the true ratio is probably nearer 0.16. The regime is positive for CAD holders but thin, about half the AUD/JPY or NOK/JPY ratio against the yen, and shrinking as the Bank of Japan hikes. In September TD Securities argued that CAD would become a more compelling carry trade funding currency relative to the yen, noting its carry-to-volatility ratio is already comparable to the Japanese yen. That is a structural reason the long-CAD/JPY carry community is smaller than in the AUD and NOK crosses. Forward points are derived from the −123.7bp rolled premium applied to 112.804.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD has a 125bp policy-rate advantage. The Bank of Canada raised its overnight target to 2.50% on 28 October and the Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on 30 October by an 8-1 vote. The BIS-compiled series still showed the Canadian rate at 2.25% on 26 October, two days before the hike, so it understates the live gap by 25bp. At two years, the Government of Canada yield of 3.31% (30 October) is about 141bp above the 1.901% JGB fixing of 29 October. At ten years the gap is about 103bp on 30 October closes (3.799% vs 2.770%). Neither bank meets in the next four weeks. The next scheduled decisions are the Bank of Canada on 9 December and the Bank of Japan on 18 December, and neither is a projection round. So the gap cannot change through policy action in this window, and the factor depends on how data and communication reprice those two meetings. The Canadian dossier thinks the market prices about 11bp too much Canadian tightening for early 2027, a mild CAD negative. The Japanese dossier thinks the roughly 75% pricing of a December Bank of Japan hike is slightly too high against its own 65%, a mild yen negative. The two errors are similar in size and cancel over this horizon.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the question is how far the 125bp gap narrows, and both legs point toward narrowing. The Bank of Japan is expected to hike to 1.50% on 18 December. Markets price nearly 75bp of Japanese tightening over twelve months, and the 22 January meeting carries the Outlook Report, the natural place to signal the next move. The Bank of Canada is tightening into a stalling economy. Third-quarter growth is tracking about 1.3% annualised against the Bank's 2.0% projection, CPI-trim and CPI-median are 1.8% and 1.9%, and the Reuters poll calls the expected cycle the shortest in 30 years, peaking at 2.75%. The 9 December decision is the only Canadian decision in the published schedule before 1 March 2027. A hold there would leave the second Canadian hike without a scheduled date inside the horizon, while the Bank of Japan has two scheduled chances to move. If the Bank of Japan reaches 1.50% and the Bank of Canada holds, the gap falls to 100bp by late December. The Canadian dossier's 40% probability that the Bank stops at 2.50% is the part the market has not priced. The effect reaches the pair mainly through the 2-year spread, which has more room to compress on the Canadian side. Holding CAD still earns about 125bp a year, so a bearish position has a running cost, which keeps confidence modest.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Most of Canada's October releases came in weaker than expected. August GDP was flat, September is estimated at -0.1%, employment fell 68,300 in September with unemployment at 6.5%, and core inflation is below target (CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%). Japan's inflation is firmer and spreading. September CPI excluding fresh food rose to 2.1%, excluding fresh food and energy it reached 2.4%, Tokyo's October core printed 2.6%, cash earnings rose 3.8% in August and the 2026 Shunto settled at 5.01%. Growth is weak in both. Japan's third quarter is expected near zero (+0.08% annualised in the JCER survey) and Canada's is tracking about 1.3%, so the growth gap is small. The decisive gap is core inflation, which runs about half a point higher in Japan. That means the Bank of Japan, not the Bank of Canada, is the one under pressure to keep tightening. Releases in the window are dense: Canadian employment on 6 November, Canadian CPI and Japanese GDP both on 16 November, Japanese national CPI on 20 November, and Canadian third-quarter GDP on 30 November, just after the window. The Canadian dossier expects a third employment decline, and the Japanese dossier gives 40% to a negative GDP print. Overall the pair is more exposed to Canadian disappointment than to Japanese, so the factor leans Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over the strategic horizon the inflation and growth mix favours the yen. The Bank of Japan's October Outlook Report keeps core CPI at 2.5% for FY2026 and raises FY2027 to 2.6%. Tankan firms expect prices to rise 2.5-2.6% a year over one to five years, and wage settlements run near 5%, so Japanese normalisation has a domestic engine. Canada's inflation overshoot comes from energy: gasoline is up 27.8% year on year while trim and median sit below 2%, wages are up only 2.3%, and housing is contracting, with September sales down 7.7% year on year. The Canadian upside risk is business inflation expectations of 3.7%, which could push core toward 2.3% if oil stays above USD 100. The main Japanese downside risk, the April 2027 food consumption-tax cut, falls outside this window. The effect reaches the pair through relative policy expectations. Firm Japanese core supports hikes on 18 December and 22 January, while soft Canadian core limits the Bank of Canada to one more hike at most. Both dossiers score this factor in the same pair direction: Bearish for CAD and Bullish for the yen.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD/JPY has moderate risk sensitivity. CAD is mildly pro-cyclical with a low risk beta anchored by its US ties, and the yen is the funding and safe-haven leg. But this cycle's main shock is an energy war, and that changes how the yen behaves as a haven. Risk indicators are weakening at the margin, not breaking. The VIX was 17.2 on 29 October, mid-range. US high-yield spreads widened 18bp in a month to 326bp, the 95th percentile of their one-year range, and the Nikkei fell 8.22% in October to about 63,290 on worries about the AI trade. For this pair the two main tail scenarios roughly cancel. An AI-led equity sell-off would unwind yen-funded carry and push the pair lower. A post-midterm escalation with Iran would lift oil, which helps CAD and hurts the yen through Japan's import bill. The pair would probably rise even as the VIX climbed, as the yen weakened during the July escalation. The carry cushion is also thin, about 125bp against estimated vol near 6.8%, so there are fewer carry positions to unwind than in AUD/JPY or NOK/JPY. With the two dominant tails pointing opposite ways for this cross, the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months this factor is a source of tail volatility rather than direction. A credit-led or equity-led sell-off would favour the yen and weigh on CAD; the Canadian dossier puts the CAD effect at a 1-2% rise in USD/CAD, so the pair would fall on both legs. A Gulf settlement would improve sentiment but cut oil by USD 15-20. That would hurt CAD's terms of trade and help the yen through a smaller import bill, so the pair would also fall despite better risk appetite. Only a risk-on with oil steady, or an escalation that lifts oil, helps the pair. The energy-war regime therefore leaves the risk distribution slightly skewed against CAD/JPY over this horizon. But that skew runs mainly through oil, which is scored under Factor 5. To avoid counting it twice, this factor is held Neutral at low confidence. Japan's large net foreign assets, about USD 3.6tn at end-2024, are the repatriation pool that would make any genuine risk-off sharp.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For this pair the two legs' positioning adds up rather than cancelling. CFTC data for the week to 27 October show leveraged funds net short 96,747 Canadian dollar contracts, within 5,748 of their 2026 extreme. Asset managers have covered to a near-flat short of 1,325. In the yen, asset managers hold a net long of 91,191 contracts, the largest of the 25 weeks since May. The legacy non-commercial net long of 101,600 is beyond the 80,000 level that has marked stretched yen longs in the past. Being short CAD and long yen at the same time means speculators are effectively short CAD/JPY through the two dollar legs, so the downside of the pair is crowded. Both dossiers independently flag the same unwind risk. A Canadian jobs beat on 6 November or a steel and auto tariff deal would squeeze the CAD short. Bank of Japan communication that leaves December open, or a negative Japanese GDP print on 16 November, would force yen longs out. A squeeze would lift CAD/JPY from both sides at once. The positions are held against the US dollar, so the exposure to this cross is inferred, which limits confidence.

The yen long is held by real money and was built steadily across two Bank of Japan hikes, so it looks like reallocation rather than a fragile trade. It would unwind only on a Bank of Japan pause, which the Japanese dossier puts at about 20%. The CAD short sits with leveraged funds and is funded by carry against the US dollar, which can last. Bilateral portfolio flows between Japan and Canada are not published often enough to be useful. Both dossiers score this factor Neutral strategically, and the bilateral reading agrees.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is where the two legs reinforce each other most directly. Higher oil is strongly positive for CAD and strongly negative for the yen, and higher LNG prices are strongly negative for the yen, so the energy shock pushes the pair up from both sides. NYMEX WTI rose 14.1% in October to USD 102.00, and JKM LNG was USD 32.84/MMBtu on 30 October, up 27.4% in a month. Japan posted a fifth straight trade deficit in September, JPY536.6bn against a JPY181.0bn forecast, with crude imports up 51.1%. Canada's August goods surplus was C$4.2bn against a C$1.5bn consensus, and its second-quarter current account swung to a C$8.84bn surplus. Two things limit the effect. The WCS discount of USD 27 under WTI caps how much of the rally Canada keeps. Japan's current account surplus of 5.03% of GDP is a cushion, although most of the investment income is reinvested abroad. Direct trade is small and runs against Canada. IMF DOTS shows Canadian exports to Japan of USD 10.9bn and imports of USD 16.2bn in 2024, a USD 5.2bn Canadian deficit. That is a minor structural source of yen demand and does not offset the terms-of-trade swing. Both trade releases in the window should show the energy effect: Canada's September data on 4 November and Japan's October data on 17 November.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the terms-of-trade gap is still the pair's strongest structural support. Winter LNG demand coincides with JKM near USD 33, projected toward USD 34 by quarter-end, while Canadian crude output is running at record levels into the price spike. That advantage lasts only as long as the Gulf supply shock does. A settlement that removed the Hormuz premium would take USD 15-20 off oil, which the Canadian dossier says costs CAD 1-1.5% against the dollar, and would remove roughly half of Japan's goods deficit. The pair would then fall on both legs. The Japanese dossier puts that settlement at about 15% within six months. Canada also faces a second external risk: the threatened 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and cars from 1 January 2027, which hits non-energy exports. Capacity matters too. Trans Mountain is full and the WCS discount reflects tight pipeline space, so Canada captures less of any further oil rally than headline WTI suggests. On balance the factor is Bullish at moderate confidence and is the clearest offset to the bearish rate and growth story.

Statistics Canada puts the year-end 2025 Japanese direct-investment position in Canada at C$46.7 billion, and nearly 75 per cent of the cars manufactured in Canada are made by Japanese companies. tactical.rationale: Four factors decide the tactical call. Inflation & Growth (0.18) is the largest directional input and is Bearish. What is priced is a December Canadian hold, a roughly 75% chance of a December Bank of Japan hike and a lasting energy premium. Our edge on each is small: slightly too much Canadian tightening priced, set against crowded downside positioning that can squeeze. strategic.score_interpretation: The score of -0.1301 is Bearish but only 0.03 beyond the -0.10 threshold. Most of the depth comes from Policy & Rates (-0.130). The rest is breadth across Guidance (-0.065), Inflation & Growth (-0.056) and Event Risk (-0.027). Against them stand External Balance (+0.110) and Fiscal (+0.037). Four factors score zero. Raising the External Balance weight made the score less bearish; at default weights it would be about -0.147.
strategic.rationale: Three factors dominate at strategic weights: Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.19 after adjustment) and Guidance (0.12). The result is a narrow Bearish score of -0.130. The rate leg is the largest negative. The Bank of Japan has two scheduled chances to hike inside the horizon: 18 December and the 22 January Outlook Report meeting. The Bank of Canada's only scheduled decision before 1 March 2027 is 9 December, where a hold is expected. So the 125bp gap is more likely to narrow toward 100bp than to widen. Guidance and Inflation & Growth reinforce this. Japanese core inflation, wages and the Board's hawkish vote shift support continued tightening, while Canadian core sits below 2% and growth is falling short of the Bank's projection. Event risk adds a small negative through the 1 January 2027 tariff deadline. The offset is External Balance, the largest positive at +0.110, because oil near USD 102 and JKM near USD 33 favour CAD over the yen through both legs. Fiscal policy adds a smaller positive through Japan's widening deficit. The two dossiers reinforce each other: the Canadian dossier is Bearish on CAD and the Japanese dossier Bullish on the yen strategically, and this cross combines both. What is priced is the gap narrowing to roughly 75-100bp over twelve months. Our edge is the 15-25bp of Canadian tightening the Canadian dossier expects to be removed, while the Japanese leg looks roughly fair. The path of least resistance is a gradual decline in the pair, with the energy premium as the main brake. Key dates are 9 December (Bank of Canada), 18 December (Bank of Japan), 1 January 2027 (US tariff deadline) and 22 January 2027 (Bank of Japan with the Outlook Report). Conviction is 2 rather than 3 for three reasons. The score is barely past the threshold. Carry of about 125bp a year works against a short. And the bullish and bearish drivers are linked through oil: a Gulf settlement would turn External Balance negative and strengthen the call, while an escalation would weaken it.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically the yen ranks 2nd of 11 in its dossier and CAD 8th in its own, a six-place gap that makes CAD/JPY one of the wider fundamental divergences on either currency's grid. Among yen longs it ranks behind short CHF/JPY, which earns positive carry for yen holders, because a CAD/JPY short pays about 125bp a year. Among CAD shorts it ranks behind short CAD/NOK and long AUD/CAD, which earn carry rather than pay it. What sets it apart is double oil exposure: of the yen longs it is the one most hurt by a Gulf escalation and most helped by a settlement.

The Bank of Japan hikes to 1.50% on 18 December and keeps core CPI above 2% in the 22 January Outlook Report
The tariff regime stays at the status quo or sees a limited escalation on 1 January
WTI holds USD 85–105
base_case.path: −205 pips (−1.82%) to 110.75 by end-January 2027, extending to 110.20 by end-April (−260 pips, −2.31%). Step-and-pause lower on central-bank dates: a Bank of Japan hike steps the pair down through the 111.41–112.16 band toward 111.40–111.80, hawkish 22 January projections carry it to 110.75, and the rising 200-week average near 110.0 by end-April slows the decline and holds the pair on top of the seven-touch support band.

A targeted US–Canada steel and auto deal lands before 1 January
A Gulf escalation pushes Brent above USD 130
Context: +250 pips (+2.21%), the bottom of the six-touch resistance band
A Gulf settlement takes USD 15–20 off oil and halves Japan's goods deficit

strategic.path_expectation: The first phase, November to early December, is the range described in the tactical section. The squeeze risk in the 6–20 November cluster is the opportunity to sell into 113.35–113.85, not a reason to chase lower from spot. The second phase runs from the 9 December Bank of Canada hold to the 18 December Bank of Japan decision. A hike should step the pair down through the 111.41–112.16 band toward 111.40–111.80, with a single 120–160 pip day around the Japanese decision. The third phase runs through the 1 January tariff deadline to the 22 January Outlook Report. If the projections are hawkish and tariffs are unresolved, the pair extends to 110.75 by late January. Pullbacks to 112.20–112.60 should be shallow and sold. From February to April, Japanese fiscal year-end repatriation and the Shunto first tally keep pressure on the pair, but the rising 200-week average, due near 110.0 by end-April, slows the decline. The pair should settle around 110.20 on top of the seven-touch support band, not break through it. The shape is step-and-pause, with the steps on central-bank dates, not a collapse.

Up to 4: the level-3 conditions plus either a 1 January tariff escalation or WTI below USD 90, with a weekly close below 110.05
Up to 5: a Gulf settlement with WTI below USD 85 and JKM below USD 20, alongside a Bank of Japan signal of 1.75% by April

Down to 1 / Neutral: a targeted tariff deal lands with WTI above USD 110

risk_reward.base_case_payoff: +205 pips / +1.82% (short at spot over three months)
risk_reward.downside_case_loss: -250 pips / -2.21% (short at spot if the upside case occurs, unstopped)
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 0.82:1 at spot; 2.7:1 from a 113.60 entry with the 114.65 stop (285 pips reward vs 105 pips risk)
risk_reward.expected_value: At spot: 0.50 × 205 + 0.25 × 380 − 0.25 × 250 = +135 pips before carry, or about +100 pips after 35 pips of carry. From the 113.60 entry with the 114.65 stop: 0.50 × 285 + 0.25 × 460 − 0.25 × 105 ≈ +231 pips before 35 pips of carry. Downside-case gain at spot (pair falls to 109.00) is +380 pips (+3.37%).
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: At spot the trade is roughly symmetric and pays carry. At the resistance entry it is clearly asymmetric in our favour, which is why patience through mid-November is part of the plan.

consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast: No bank survey for CAD/JPY could be found; the implied view comes from crossing leg surveys. Reuters FX poll (3 September) has USD/CAD at 1.39 in three months and 1.36 in twelve; Bloomberg survey (1 October) has USD/JPY at 156 at end-Q4 2026 and 150.5 at end-Q3 2027. Together they imply a mild CAD/JPY decline of roughly 0.5% by year-end (about 112.2) and about 2% over twelve months (about 111.1 interpolated to end-April 2027). MUFG's USD/JPY path implies slightly more.
consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast_source: Implied by crossing leg surveys cited in the dossiers: Reuters FX poll of 3 September 2026 (USD/CAD), Bloomberg survey of 1 October 2026 (USD/JPY) and MUFG's USD/JPY path. No bank survey of CAD/JPY itself found.
consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Neutral: no directional edge over four weeks, with squeeze risk to the upside from crowded positioning.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish: the pair falls as the policy gap narrows and Japanese guidance proves more credible. Price levels are set in the trade plan.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: In line with the implied consensus on direction strategically (but more bearish and earlier on levels); tactically we are Neutral where the implied consensus leans slightly lower
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Our 110.75 for late January sits about 145 pips below the implied three-month cross; our 110.20 for end-April sits about 90 pips below the implied six-month cross
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: We share the implied consensus direction but reach it differently. The Reuters poll's CAD view assumes trade tensions eventually fade and CAD strengthens against the dollar. The Bloomberg survey expects steady yen strength. Crossed, they give a small decline that relies entirely on the yen leg. We reach a bearish CAD/JPY through both legs. The Canadian dossier expects the Bank of Canada to stop early and sees a heavier tariff tail into 1 January 2027. The Japanese dossier expects two Bank of Japan hikes in six months. Where we are more cautious than consensus is energy: we give the terms-of-trade gap more weight than either leg survey implies, which is why conviction is only 2. Price levels against consensus: crossing 1.39 USD/CAD with 156 USD/JPY gives an implied year-end CAD/JPY near 112.2, and interpolating both surveys to end-April 2027 gives roughly 111.1. We are therefore more bearish and earlier than consensus, because we add a Canadian leg the polls do not have. Published aggregations lean the other way: one aggregation of six providers puts the Q4 2026 consensus at 113.84, with a low of 109.89 and a high of 119.05, and 114.25 mid-2027. The constituents are not identified, so we give it less weight than the bank leg surveys, but it marks the market's upward lean on the energy story. Where we disagree with our own call: through October the pair made six consecutive higher lows and reclaimed its 50-day, and the energy rally that drives it has not faded. That structure is not evidence about fundamentals and does not change the score. It is the reason the plan waits for a better entry and treats a weekly close above 114.56 as the point at which the strategic view must be reviewed.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The pair falls with both legs contributing. The carry cost of about 125bp a year is small against estimated vol near 7%. A move to 110.20 pays 260 pips from spot and about 360 pips against the six-provider aggregation.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the Gulf premium persists or escalates and a US-Canada tariff deal lands, both legs move against the view. Crowded short-CAD and long-yen positioning would then amplify a squeeze higher in the pair. The 114.65 stop limits the loss from the preferred entry to 105 pips.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The two horizons differ for mechanical reasons. Over four weeks neither bank meets, positioning is crowded against the pair and the energy windfall shows up in two trade releases, which offsets weak Canadian data. Over one to three months the Bank of Japan's 18 December and 22 January decisions fall inside the window against one expected Canadian hold on 9 December. Rates and guidance therefore carry the score, and External Balance is the only material offset.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 9 December Bank of Canada decision and the 18 December Bank of Japan decision, followed by the 22 January 2027 Bank of Japan meeting with the Outlook Report. Earlier, the mid-November cluster (6-20 November) decides whether crowded positioning gets squeezed first.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Stay flat or range-neutral through the 6-20 November data and communication cluster, when squeeze risk is highest. Build the strategic bearish view into the December decisions. Levels: trade the range 111.40–113.85 tactically. Build the strategic short at 113.35–113.85 after 20 November, or on a daily close below 111.41. Use a daily close above 114.65 as the stop, with targets at 111.80 and 110.75 by late January and 110.20 by end-April.

forward_vs_spot.forward_1m: 112.688 (−11.6 pips, −0.10%); our expected 1M rate is 112.50, an edge of −19 pips (pair lower than forward), under a third of a normal day and not tradeable
forward_vs_spot.edge_6m: −191 pips. Forwards price only the carry drift: the pair about 70 pips lower over six months, with no fundamental move. Our path adds about 190 pips beyond that at six months. Most of the edge arrives with the December and January central-bank steps, so it grows quickly to three months and slowly after. Of the 260-pip spot move expected over six months, about 70 pips is already in the forward, which is why a forward sale and a spot short are close substitutes here.

catalysts.rationale: The midterms open a window in which US strikes on Iran become possible. For this cross an escalation is bullish, because higher oil helps CAD and hurts the yen. The result also shapes US–Canada tariff politics, and the Tokyo holiday thins liquidity on the day.

This is the first full month with WTI above USD 90. The Canadian dossier expects the surplus to stay above C$3bn after August's C$4.2bn, confirming the terms-of-trade windfall that is CAD's main support against an energy-importing yen.

catalysts.event: Canadian federal budget and 10-year JGB auction
catalysts.rationale: Two fiscal tests on the same day. The Canadian budget is expected to confirm a deficit of about C$65bn and should be neutral. A weak JGB auction would revive the Japanese term-premium story, which in this cycle has weakened the yen.

catalysts.event: Canadian Labour Force Survey (October) and Governor Ueda's remarks
catalysts.rationale: A third straight job decline would erode early-2027 Bank of Canada hike pricing. Ueda's first remarks after the Outlook Report can move December Bank of Japan odds by 10–15 points. A jobs beat is the main trigger for a CAD short squeeze, which would test 113.37.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Summary of Opinions and Bank of Canada summary of deliberations (week of 9 November)
catalysts.rationale: Both accounts land in the same week. A Japanese summary showing several members ready to hike, or a Canadian summary discussing a December pause, would weigh on the pair. The opposite readings would trigger the two-legged covering described under Factor 4.

catalysts.event: Canadian CPI (October) and Japanese Q3 GDP, first estimate
catalysts.rationale: Canadian core below 2% would undercut a second hike, which is bearish for the pair. A negative Japanese GDP print, which the Japanese dossier puts at 40%, would revive the Bank of Japan's dovish wing and could squeeze yen longs, which is bullish for the pair.
October includes JKM's 27% monthly rise and the start of winter LNG buying. The Japanese dossier expects a deficit of JPY0.8–1.2tn against September's JPY0.54tn, a direct yen drain.
Tokyo's 2.6% core points to national core of 2.3–2.5%. A print of 2.4% or higher would cement a December hike and support the narrowing gap at the centre of the strategic view.

Industry data put Q3 growth near 1.3% annualised against the Bank's 2.0%. A print below 1.5% confirms the shortfall into 9 December. August GDP was flat and September is estimated at -0.1%, so a weak print would add to the Canadian leg's growth drag.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision (no projection round)
catalysts.rationale: The Canadian dossier expects a hold at 2.50% (65%). It is the only Canadian decision before 1 March 2027, so a hold with softer guidance leaves the second hike without a scheduled date inside the horizon.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting
catalysts.rationale: A 25bp hike to 1.50% is about 75% priced and would cut the policy gap to 100bp. A hold would be the largest yen-negative event in the horizon and would put 115.30 in play.

catalysts.event: Threatened increase of US tariffs on Canadian steel and cars to 50%
catalysts.rationale: Escalation (25%) would hit non-energy exports and Japanese auto investment in Canada. A targeted deal (35%) would release the tariff discount and is the main bullish risk to the strategic view.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: A projection round, which moves the pair more than a plain statement. Hawkish projections would extend the narrowing of the gap beyond what is priced and carry the base case to 110.75.

invalidators.condition: The Bank of Japan holds on 18 December and January hike pricing falls below 40%
invalidators.mechanism: The strategic case rests on two Japanese chances to narrow a 125bp gap against one Canadian hold. Without the December hike the gap stays at 125bp into February.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Bank of Japan decision and OIS-implied January pricing

invalidators.condition: A targeted US–Canada agreement cuts Section 232 steel or car tariffs and withdraws the 1 January 2027 threat
invalidators.mechanism: The Canadian leg loses its tariff discount and Japanese auto investment in Canada regains its US access. Only the yen side of the bearish case would remain.

invalidators.condition: WTI holds above USD 110 with the WCS discount narrower than USD 15, and JKM stays above USD 40 for four weeks
invalidators.mechanism: The double-sided energy channel would outweigh the rate and guidance factors at the 0.19 External Balance weight.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: NYMEX WTI, Hardisty WCS differential, JKM

invalidators.condition: Canadian employment rises more than 30,000 cumulatively across the October and November reports and CPI-trim/median averages above 2.3%
invalidators.mechanism: A firm Bank of Canada hike in early 2027 would keep the gap at 125bp even after a Japanese hike.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Labour Force Survey and Bank of Canada core measures

invalidators.condition: The Canada–Japan 2-year yield spread widens above 165bp from about 141bp for ten sessions
invalidators.mechanism: The front end would be pricing the gap widening, not narrowing, which reverses Factor 1.

invalidators.condition: CAD/JPY posts a weekly close above 116.41, the top of the six-touch resistance band
invalidators.mechanism: A close there would mean the energy and positioning forces have overwhelmed the rate path, and the trade plan's risk assumptions would no longer hold.

signposts.current_level: about +141bp (Government of Canada 2-year 3.31% on 30 October vs JGB 2-year 1.901% on 29 October)
signposts.bilateral_importance: The pair's rate channel runs through the front end, and the two banks have opposite schedules in the horizon. This spread captures both sides of the narrowing case, which neither dollar spread does on its own.

signposts.indicator: Bank of Japan December hike pricing
signposts.confirms_if: above 85% after the Summary of Opinions and national CPI
signposts.bilateral_importance: The 18 December meeting is the first scheduled narrowing of the CAD–yen gap. It also decides whether the crowded yen long is rewarded or liquidated.

signposts.indicator: Canadian core inflation (CPI-trim and CPI-median average)
signposts.confirms_if: at or below 2.0% in the October and November releases
signposts.bilateral_importance: The core-inflation gap with Japan (2.4% excluding fresh food and energy) is the decisive Factor 2 differential. Canadian core above 2.3% would close it.

signposts.indicator: WTI, WCS differential and JKM LNG
signposts.current_level: WTI USD 102.00 (29 October); WCS USD 27.00 under WTI (16 October); JKM USD 32.84/MMBtu (30 October)
signposts.confirms_if: WTI below USD 90 or JKM below USD 25
signposts.invalidates_if: WTI above USD 110 with WCS narrower than USD 15, or JKM above USD 40, for four weeks
signposts.bilateral_importance: Energy moves both legs in the same pair direction, so the pair's sensitivity is roughly double that of either dollar pair.

signposts.indicator: Combined speculative positioning (CAD leveraged funds and JPY legacy non-commercial)
signposts.current_level: CAD leveraged funds −96,747; JPY legacy +101,600; JPY asset managers +91,191 (week to 27 October)
signposts.confirms_if: the JPY legacy long eases below 80,000 and the CAD leveraged short below 70,000 without the pair closing above 114.56, meaning the squeeze risk burns off without damage
signposts.invalidates_if: the CAD leveraged short falls below 50,000 while the pair closes above 114.56, meaning the two-legged squeeze has started
signposts.bilateral_importance: The two books add up to a short in this cross that neither dollar pair shows on its own.
This is the yen half of the terms-of-trade channel. Against an energy exporter it is the cleanest measure of the drain that props the pair up.

signposts.indicator: US–Canada steel and auto tariff negotiations
signposts.current_level: Section 232 steel up to 50%, cars 25%; 50% on C$20bn of goods since 22 August; targeted talks reported 26–27 October
signposts.confirms_if: no agreement by 15 December, or 50% steel and car tariffs confirmed for 1 January 2027
signposts.invalidates_if: a signed targeted agreement lowering steel or car tariffs
signposts.bilateral_importance: Japanese automakers build most of Canada's cars, so the tariff outcome hits Canadian exports and Japanese direct investment in Canada together.

assumptions: Price series: daily closing prices, 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30, with spot at 112.804 on the 30 October close. The valuation date of 1 November is a Sunday, so no trading sessions are missing between spot and valuation. The series contains weekday bars only.

Data quality: the full history behind the series runs to 4,919 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30, with 1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars. The 130 daily sessions shown cover the one-to-six-month strategic horizon.

Moving averages and zones: the 50-, 100- and 200-day and 200-week averages and the support and resistance zones are computed over that full history. Averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Zones cluster weekly and monthly swing closes and are ranked by touch count. Zone distances are measured to each band's midpoint, and near-edge distances are given alongside. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days, and ATR(14) is 65 pips.

Policy rates: the Bank of Canada rate is taken as 2.50%, from its 28 October 2026 announcement. The policy-rate series received with the price data still showed 2.25% as of 26 October, before the hike, giving a stale 100bp differential. The live differential is 125bp.

Ten-year yields: the 10-year yields received with the price data are monthly readings dated 1 September 2026 (Canada 3.8825%, Japan 3.05%, a gap of 83bp) and are not used as live levels. Live ten-year comparisons use the 30 October closes cited in the dossiers (3.799% and 2.770%).

Implied volatility: the CAD/JPY vol of 6.764% at 98.7 days is an estimate, not a quote. It is built from CME-listed Canadian dollar and yen futures options with a realised correlation of 0.4855, observed 29 October 2026. No CAD/JPY option is listed, the method has run low in past checks, and the figure should be read as a floor. The one-month estimate is 6.327% and the six-month 7.047%. IV percentile is not available.

Forward points: derived from the rolled futures premium of about 124bp a year (CME Canadian dollar and yen futures, November to December contracts, observed 29 October). That premium includes the cross-currency basis and is reported alongside the policy differential, not as a substitute for it.
Positioning: CFTC positioning is held against the US dollar in both currencies. The pair-level crowding described is inferred by combining the two legs.

Consensus: the bank consensus for CAD/JPY is implied by crossing the leg surveys cited in the dossiers. No bank survey of CAD/JPY itself could be found. One published multi-provider aggregation is shown for context and flagged for unclear provenance, and model-extrapolation forecast sites were excluded.

Central-bank calendar: the published schedule shows no Bank of Canada decision between 9 December 2026 and 1 March 2027. The second Canadian hike that markets price for early 2027 therefore has no confirmed date inside the strategic horizon.

Bilateral trade: IMF DOTS goods trade for 2024 differs depending on which side reports it (Canadian imports from Japan USD 16.2bn vs Japanese exports to Canada USD 11.2bn). Canada's reported figures are used for the net balance of −USD 5.2bn.

Price data and factor stances: no trailing returns, moving averages, ranges or support and resistance levels were used for any factor stance. Factor 9 uses only volatility evidence. Trend, levels, entries, targets, stops and sizing are built from the price data, and the 200-week convergence timing uses its supplied slope of 4.89 pips a week.

Probabilities: probabilities for central-bank decisions, tariff outcomes and geopolitical tails come from the CAD and JPY dossiers unless described as market pricing. Scenario probabilities follow the 50/25/25 framework convention.

Horizons: the tactical horizon runs to about 27–29 November 2026. The strategic scenarios are set to end-January 2027, covering the 9 December, 18 December and 22 January decisions, with an end-April 2027 extension used in the forward decomposition.
Weights: the weight adjustments are documented in the Synthesis table and sum to 1.00 on both horizons.
